A family on a fixed income cannot simply decide to consume less heat in January, and they cannot decide to eat less than they already do. When prices rise across the whole basket at once, the usual advice about shopping around collapses, because there is nowhere to shop around to. Every supermarket has raised prices. The measures announced so far are welcome as far as they go, but they are calibrated for a much milder shock than the one arriving. A rebate spread over five years, repayable, is not support; it is a loan dressed up in the language of support. What is needed is targeted help that reaches people before the arrears build, because once arrears build, the costs compound: disconnection, debt collection, and in too many cases eviction. I would also press the point about uprating. If benefits are uprated on a figure taken from last September while inflation runs at five per cent or more now, we are legislating a real-terms cut for the poorest households in the middle of a cost crisis, and we are doing it deliberately, with full knowledge of the numbers. That is a choice. It can be unmade. I hope the Government will look again at the uprating decision, at the energy support package, and at the position of households on prepayment meters, who pay the most and have the least.

People who are entitled to support should not have to litigate to receive it, and a regime that depends on judicial review to function is a regime that has already failed the people it was designed for. Litigation is slow, it is expensive, and it is available in practice only to those who can find a solicitor willing to take the case. So while the legal backstop matters, and I am glad it is there, I do not regard it as the primary mechanism. The primary mechanism is clear guidance, issued early, written in language that a busy officer in a local authority can actually apply on a Tuesday afternoon with a queue of cases in front of them. My officials are working on that guidance now, and I have asked that it be published in draft so that authorities and representative bodies can comment before it is finalised. Alongside that, we will be monitoring compliance directly rather than waiting for complaints. Data returns will tell us where duties are being discharged and where they are not, and I expect to publish that information so the House can see it too. Where a public authority is falling short, my strong preference is to work with it, understand whether the problem is capacity, understanding or systems, and fix the cause. Where the failure is persistent and there is no willingness to remedy it, stronger measures are available and I will not hesitate to use them. I would also say to the House that we should be honest that duties of this kind carry a resource implication. Authorities are being asked to do something new. If we will the end, we must be prepared to will the means, and I will be making that case within Government.

There are procedures for dealing with the conduct of officials. There are appeal mechanisms. There are ministers who are accountable to this House and who can be questioned here as often as we like. But there is a difference between criticising a decision and putting a named official at the bar of the House. The first is our job. The second is an abandonment of it, because it lets ministers hide behind the person they instructed. If the decision was wrong, the minister answers for it. I would rather not legislate if a voluntary approach delivers, because legislation in this area is difficult to get right and easy to get wrong, and the technology moves faster than any Bill can. But the honest position is that we have been having this conversation with the companies for some years now and the pace of improvement has not matched the scale of the harm. Removal times have come down for the most egregious categories, which I acknowledge, but they remain far too slow for material that is causing active distress to identifiable individuals, and the reporting mechanisms are still, frankly, designed for the convenience of the platform rather than for the person in crisis at the other end of the phone. My hon. Friend will know from her casework, as I know from mine, what it is like to sit with a parent who has spent three weeks trying to get an image of their child taken down. So the question is not whether the companies can do this. They can. They deploy extraordinary engineering resources when the commercial incentive points in that direction, and content that infringes copyright disappears within hours. The question is whether they will do it without being compelled, and the evidence of the last decade suggests the answer is that some will and some will not. That points towards a statutory duty with a regulator behind it, and a penalty regime with enough weight to register on a balance sheet measured in tens of billions. I would add one further point. Whatever we do domestically will only go so far, because these are global services. That means working with counterparts in Europe, in the Commonwealth and with the United States to align expectations, so that a company cannot simply arbitrage between jurisdictions and treat compliance here as an optional local cost.

dogs are killed for meat every year, many of them stolen family pets, many of them transported for days in conditions that would not be tolerated for any animal in this country. I want to be clear at the outset about what this Bill does and does not do. It does not lecture other countries about their cuisine, and it is not an exercise in cultural finger-pointing. Several of the most effective campaigns against this trade have been led from within the countries where it takes place, by activists who face real risk in doing so, and their argument is not that the practice is foreign but that it is cruel and that it is a public health hazard. Rabies transmission follows these supply chains. So does the theft that supplies them. What the Bill does is close a gap in our own law. It is currently not an offence in this country to consume dog meat. It is an offence to sell it, because of food safety and animal by-product regulation, and it is an offence to kill a dog for that purpose, because of our animal welfare legislation. But the act of consumption itself sits outside the law, and so does possession or transport for that purpose. I accept immediately that this is not a widespread practice here. Members may reasonably ask why we should legislate for something that happens rarely or perhaps not at all. My answer is twofold. First, a loophole that is currently unused is still a loophole, and the enforcement bodies have told me that the absence of a clear offence complicates prosecutions that would otherwise be straightforward. Second, and more importantly, we ask other countries to act on this trade. Our credibility in doing so is stronger when our own statute book is unambiguous. Several jurisdictions have already legislated in exactly these terms.

Pursuing economic crime makes you unpopular with people who have very good lawyers, and both of them have shown considerable persistence in the face of that. I want to make three points. The first is about resourcing. We talk about enforcement as though it were a matter of will alone, but the arithmetic is stark. The agencies charged with investigating complex fraud and money laundering are operating with budgets that have been flat or falling in real terms while the volume and sophistication of the crime has grown enormously. A single contested case can consume years of specialist time and run to costs that make the responsible officials nervous about starting at all. Until we deal with the cost-risk asymmetry, where the agency faces ruin if it loses and the defendant faces a fine that is a rounding error if it wins, we will keep seeing cases quietly dropped. The second is about company formation. It remains far too easy to register a company in this country with directors who do not exist, at addresses that turn out to be a mailbox above a shop, and to use that company to move money. Reform of the registry has been promised repeatedly. Verification of identity at the point of registration is the single highest-value change available to us and it does not require a new international agreement or a change of political direction; it requires the Government to do the thing they have already said they will do. Third, on property. The register of overseas entities was a real achievement, but a register is only useful if somebody reads it, checks it and acts on discrepancies. At present there is very little evidence of that happening at scale, and the discrepancy reporting regime has no teeth behind it whatsoever.

The present rule was written for a chamber in which members were physically present in large numbers throughout the sitting day, and in which finding five colleagues to rise was a trivial matter that took no time at all. That places the right where it belongs, with the party caucus and ultimately with the voters who sent them here, rather than with the accident of attendance. I understand the objection. Members will say that this makes recorded votes easier and that we already spend a great deal of time voting. I would answer that the remedy for excessive voting is electronic voting or grouped votes at a fixed hour, both of which we should consider, and not the preservation of a procedural obstacle that operates arbitrarily. be clear, in everything we say and everything we broadcast, that our quarrel is with the regime and not with the population. That is not a sentimental point; it is a strategic one. The Russian state has spent twenty years constructing a narrative in which the West is permanently and instinctively hostile to Russians as a people, and every clumsy formulation on our side is harvested as evidence for it. We should refuse to supply that evidence. In practice that means several things. It means keeping open the channels through which Russians can hear something other than state television: the BBC Russian service, which should be funded properly rather than left to survive on the margins of the World Service budget, and support for the independent Russian-language outlets now operating in exile in Riga, Vilnius, Tbilisi and Berlin. It means resisting calls to close our doors to Russians fleeing conscription or persecution. A country that has just criminalised the word war is producing refugees, and those refugees are, by definition, people who reject what is being done in their name. Turning them away serves no purpose except the Kremlin's. It also means being precise about sanctions. Measures aimed at the central bank, at the export of sensitive technology, and at the personal assets of those who have profited from the regime are proportionate and effective. Measures that fall indiscriminately on ordinary consumers achieve very little militarily while confirming the propaganda. I accept the distinction is not always clean, and that some general economic pain is unavoidable given the scale of what we are doing, but the direction of travel should be towards precision, not away from it. Finally, we should say plainly and repeatedly that there is a future in which Russia is a normal European neighbour, because if we never describe that future, nobody inside Russia will work towards it.

If a Member believes that a statement made at the Dispatch Box was inaccurate, the proper course is to raise it with the Minister directly, to seek a correction, and if none is forthcoming, to pursue the matter through the mechanisms available: written questions, an application for an urgent question, or a debate. Those mechanisms have teeth, provided Members use them with persistence. I would add, for the benefit of the House generally and not in relation to this particular exchange, that I have noticed a growing tendency to use points of order as a vehicle for continuing arguments that have concluded. Points of order are for matters of order. I have been generous, perhaps overly generous, in allowing latitude, because I would always rather Members got something off their chest here than nursed a grievance. But the currency is devalued by overuse. I hope the House will bear that in mind. We come now to the ten-minute rule motion.

It is difficult to reconcile that campaign, which was genuine and well intentioned and which reached an enormous audience, with the commercial arrangements that surround the game at every level below the elite. My hon. Friend has put her finger on the inconsistency. Clubs are perfectly willing to speak about the wellbeing of players and supporters, and then to sign agreements whose entire business model depends on a small proportion of people losing far more than they can afford. The evidence on that is not seriously contested any more. A large majority of the revenue comes from a small minority of customers, and that minority is disproportionately made up of people already in difficulty. That is not a marketing failure; it is the model working as designed. The Government's position is that the current regulatory framework was written for a world of betting shops and telephone accounts, and it has not kept pace with an environment in which the product is on the phone in your pocket, available at three in the morning, with no closing time and no member of staff to notice that you have been there for six hours. The review we have launched will look at affordability checks, at the design features that drive prolonged play, at advertising and sponsorship, and at the adequacy of the current levy arrangements for treatment and research. On sponsorship specifically, I would say to the football authorities that they have an opportunity to act before they are acted upon. A voluntary move away from front-of-shirt gambling sponsorship, agreed collectively so that no single club is disadvantaged, would be far preferable to a statutory ban imposed on a timetable they do not control. I have said this to them privately and I am happy to say it publicly. My hon. Friend should keep pressing, because pressure of this kind is what moves these things.

The combination means that the tender price has become close to meaningless as a predictor of final cost, and that nobody learns anything from one project to the next, because the information that would allow learning is locked up in a settlement agreement. I asked the Department for a schedule of the twenty largest capital projects completed in the last decade, showing tender price and final outturn. I was told that the information is not held centrally in that form. I find that extraordinary. If we do not hold it centrally, we cannot know whether the problem is getting better or worse, and we cannot identify which contractors, or for that matter which client bodies, are consistently associated with overruns. I would ask the witnesses whether they accept that this information should be collected and published as a matter of routine, what would prevent it being done, and whether there is any objection in principle to publishing the outturn figure and the tender figure for every project above a threshold, say ten million euro.

But I would caution against making progress on any one of them a precondition for talking about the others, because that is a recipe for talking about nothing. What the committee found, hearing from homeowners, engineers and the regulatory bodies, is that these are not a series of unrelated misfortunes. They share a common cause. We moved, over a period of about fifteen years, to a system of self-certification in which the person paid by the developer certified that the developer's work complied with the regulations, and in which the local authority inspection rate fell to a token level. The reforms introduced after 2014 improved matters but did not change the underlying architecture, because certification remains a private contractual matter with the enforcement body one step removed. The committee's central recommendation is therefore structural: an independent building control authority with its own inspectors, its own budget, and a statutory minimum inspection rate that cannot be squeezed when local authority finances tighten. Alongside that, we recommend latent defects insurance as a condition of sale for new dwellings, which is standard in several European jurisdictions and which puts the cost of poor construction back onto the party best able to prevent it. On redress for existing homeowners, the committee was unanimous that the current schemes are too narrow, too slow and too heavily weighted towards proving eligibility rather than fixing homes. The evidence of the last decade is unambiguous: production rose while pipeline capacity was constrained, and the differential was carried by rail, at higher cost, higher emissions per barrel moved, and higher risk. The only thing the constraint achieved was a price discount that transferred billions of dollars from Canadian producers and Canadian treasuries to refiners in another country. I would also make a point about the standard being applied. When we assess a pipeline, we conduct a review that runs for years and considers effects on species, on water, on Indigenous rights and on downstream emissions. We have seen this repeatedly: cap the headline charge and the fee reappears as an administration charge, or the product is restructured so that it falls into a different category, or the provider withdraws from the segment altogether and consumers who had a poor deal now have no deal at all. That last outcome is the one that concerns me most, because it is invisible. Nobody writes to their Member of Parliament to say that a product they have never heard of is no longer available to them. I do not think it is, for two reasons. The first is practical. The multiculturalism funding program supports organizations on the ground: the Haitian community centre in Montreal North, the Portuguese seniors' association, the groups that run language classes and legal clinics and youth programs. Those organizations do not have a provincial equivalent of comparable scale to turn to. Exempting the province from the Act does not transfer the money; it removes the eligibility. The people who would notice first are not constitutional theorists but the volunteers who would find their annual application returned. The second reason is about what a federal statute is for. The Act does not require any province to adopt a particular integration policy. It commits the federal government, in its own dealings, to a set of principles. Removing one province from that commitment means the federal government would be operating on one basis in ten provinces and another basis in the eleventh, which raises immediate questions about federal institutions, federal employment and federal services in that province. I have not heard an answer to those questions from the sponsors of the motion, and I would genuinely like to hear one, because if there is a workable answer I will listen to it.

That practice serves villages across a wide geography, with branch surgeries that open two mornings a week, and its partners have been trying to recruit a third GP for two years without a single applicant. This is the pattern across rural England and it is worth being precise about the causes, because the debate frequently reduces to a call for more doctors in general, and more doctors in general will not solve it. We are actually training more doctors than we ever have. The problem is distribution and the problem is the partnership model. A young doctor finishing training is being asked, in a rural setting, to take on unlimited liability as a partner, often including a share of a building that is difficult to sell, in a practice with a list size and a demographic profile that guarantees a heavy workload, in a location where their partner may struggle to find work and where the secondary school may be twenty miles away. Set against a salaried role in a larger urban practice with defined sessions, it is not a close contest, and we should stop being surprised by the outcome. What might help? First, the targeted enhanced recruitment scheme has worked where it has been applied, and it should be extended to more rural areas rather than being rationed. Second, we should look seriously at the premises problem, because the last-partner-standing liability is a genuine deterrent and it is within our power to address it. Third, the funding formula. The Carr-Hill adjustment does not adequately capture rurality, and it does not capture the cost of running branch surgeries at all. A practice covering three hundred square miles has costs that a practice covering three square miles does not, and the formula treats them as equivalent. I would ask the Minister when the formula was last reviewed and whether a review is planned.

The evidence from those jurisdictions that have legislated is that a small but real number of people experience symptoms that cannot be controlled, and a larger number experience a loss of dignity and independence that they find intolerable and that no clinical intervention addresses. Those people currently have three options: to endure it, to end their lives alone and often violently while still physically able, or to travel abroad if they have the money and the mobility, which makes this in part a question about class. The case against rests on the risk to people who do not wish to die but who may come to feel they ought to. That risk is real and I will not minimise it. We spent decades building a social consensus that drinking and driving is unacceptable, and it worked. It genuinely worked. A generation grew up who would not consider it, who would take somebody's keys off them at a party, and the numbers fell year after year. We have not built anything comparable around the phone, and the reason, I think, is that we have not yet accepted in our own minds that it is the same category of thing. Everybody in this chamber has looked at a screen at a red light. I have. It does not feel like impairment. It feels like efficiency. That is the problem. The research on this is unambiguous and it has been for twenty years. Reaction time under phone distraction is comparable to reaction time at the legal blood alcohol limit, and it is worse for texting. The brain does not multitask; it switches, and the switching cost is measured in car lengths. Hands-free is better but it is not safe, because the impairment is cognitive rather than manual. That finding is uncomfortable because it undermines the compromise most of us have settled into. So what should we do? Enforcement matters and I support increased penalties, but enforcement alone will not do it, because the probability of being caught for any given instance is close to zero and drivers know it. What changed drinking and driving was social unacceptability, which came from sustained public education over a very long period, aimed particularly at young drivers, combined with technology. Vehicles can detect phone use. Phones can detect driving. The technical means to make this behaviour difficult exist and are not being required.

The Deputy is right that the current arrangement is not working as intended and that the review, when it reports, will need to say so plainly rather than describe a system in the terms in which it was originally conceived. There are two distinct problems and they require different remedies. The first is the eligibility criteria, which were drawn tightly at the outset for good reasons of cost control and which have not been revisited since, with the result that the qualifying thresholds have drifted well behind the underlying costs they were designed to cover. A threshold set in nominal terms five years ago is a substantially tighter threshold today. That is a straightforward indexation problem and it can be fixed in the estimates. It concerns the interaction between this scheme and two others administered by different bodies, where a person can be eligible under one, ineligible under another, and required to apply separately to each with substantially the same documentation. I have met people who have simply given up part way through, and I do not blame them. The Deputy has raised individual cases with me and in at least two of them the explanation for the refusal was, when we traced it back, a discrepancy in how the same income was assessed by two different offices. That is the distinction I want the House to hold onto, because it is frequently lost in the way we discuss adaptation. Adaptation is often presented as an alternative to mitigation, a pragmatic acceptance that we should protect ourselves rather than pursue emissions targets that others will not meet. But adaptation has a ceiling. You can raise a sea wall, at cost, up to a point. You cannot adapt to the loss of a stable monsoon. You cannot adapt to a wet-bulb temperature that exceeds the limit of human thermoregulation for weeks at a time, other than by leaving. So the case for mitigation is not weakened by the fact that some damage is now locked in; it is strengthened, because mitigation is what determines whether the damage stays within the range that adaptation can address. For this country, the practical implications are concrete. We should be planning our coastal defences on the upper end of the projections rather than the central estimate, because the cost asymmetry is enormous: overbuild and you have wasted money, underbuild and you lose the settlement. We should be revising the flood maps far more frequently than we currently do, and we should stop granting permission on land that those maps will show as at risk within the lifetime of the buildings concerned. We should be planning for the agricultural consequences of longer dry periods punctuated by more intense rainfall, which is the pattern the models converge on. And we should be honest with the public about which places we will defend and which we will not, because that conversation is coming and postponing it does not make it easier. Other countries have begun it. We have not.

It contains its own provisions for review, for democratic consent, and for modification by agreement. Those provisions are not decoration; they were negotiated because both sides understood that arrangements imposed on a community that has not consented to them will not hold. What has gone wrong is not primarily the text. It is that the implementation has proceeded as though Northern Ireland were an ordinary external border rather than the internal supply chain of a single country, with the result that a supermarket in Belfast is completing paperwork for a lorry of chilled goods leaving a depot in Warrington destined for its own store. The risk to the single market from that movement is, in any honest assessment, negligible. Applying the full apparatus to it is a choice, not a legal necessity, and it is a choice that has generated precisely the political instability that all parties said they wished to avoid. The answer, in my view, lies in the green lane approach with real-time data sharing: give the European Union better visibility of what is actually moving than it has today, in exchange for removing the checks on goods that demonstrably remain within the United Kingdom. That is not a British trick. It is how modern customs risk management works everywhere else in the world. Where I would caution the House is against the suggestion that unilateral action offers a shortcut. It does not. It would forfeit the good faith on which any durable arrangement depends, it would jeopardise the wider relationship, and it would not in fact deliver certainty to any business, because a business cannot plan around a legal position that is being contested in international law.

I find it difficult to argue that the principle was sound when the money was flowing towards us and unsound now. There is a second argument, which is one of self-interest rather than principle. Since then we have had eight consecutive deficits, in periods of growth and in periods of contraction alike, which tells us something important: the deficit is not a response to circumstances but a preference. A government that runs a deficit in a downturn is doing what the textbooks recommend. A government that runs a deficit through a sustained expansion, with employment at record levels and revenues at record levels, has simply decided that it prefers to spend more than it collects and to send the bill forward. The consequence is now arriving in the form of debt service costs, which are the fastest-growing line in the estimates and which will shortly exceed the health transfer to the provinces. Let us be clear about what that means, because it is easy to let a number like that pass. Every dollar spent servicing debt buys nothing. It builds no housing, treats no patient, trains no apprentice. It is money transferred from Canadian taxpayers, disproportionately from future Canadian taxpayers, to bondholders. And it is not discretionary; it cannot be reviewed or reprioritized, because the alternative is default. Every year that line grows, the room available to any future government, of any party, to respond to any crisis, shrinks. I want to anticipate the response, which will be that the debt-to-GDP ratio remains favourable by international comparison. That was a more persuasive argument when interest rates were near zero. The stock of debt was accumulated on the assumption that money would remain cheap indefinitely, and that assumption has now been tested. The refinancing occurring over the next three years will happen at rates several points higher than the maturing issues.

Several Members raised the question of loneliness, and I want to say that I think this is the issue we have most consistently underestimated. We have tended to treat it as a social matter rather than a health one, and the evidence does not support that separation. Second, on access to psychological therapies for older people, several Members correctly identified that referral rates fall sharply with age. The reasons are partly on the demand side, in that a generation was raised not to discuss these matters, and partly on the supply side, in that services designed around a working-age population are less accessible to someone who does not drive and cannot use an online booking system. There is also, I am afraid, an element of therapeutic pessimism among some professionals, an assumption that depression in an eighty-year-old is understandable rather than treatable. I want to address the defence that has been offered, which is that the relationship was a personal friendship of long standing and therefore fell within the exception provided in the Act. The Commissioner considered that argument and rejected it, and the reasoning is worth putting on the record because it applies well beyond this case. The exception exists so that a public office holder is not required to recuse themselves from every decision touching anybody they have ever met. It is not a mechanism by which a friendship with a person who has substantial business before the Crown converts that person's interests into a private matter. If it were, the Act would be unworkable, because every well-connected person in the country would be somebody's friend. The test is whether the office holder had an opportunity to improperly further another person's private interests, and the Commissioner found that he did, on two occasions, and did not withdraw. I also want to say something about the response, which has been that the Prime Minister accepts the findings and will clear future travel with the Commissioner in advance. That is not accountability; it is an undertaking to seek permission next time. The Act contains no penalty for a contravention of this kind, which is a defect this House should address, but the absence of a statutory penalty does not mean the absence of consequence. The consequence is supposed to be political, delivered here, and it is entirely within the power of this chamber to insist on it. What we should not do is treat the report as the conclusion of the matter simply because it has been tabled.

That is an intolerable position to put a company in, and it is not one they can resolve themselves. A bank cannot choose between compliance with European law and compliance with American law; it can only choose which regulator to disappoint, and the answer is invariably the one with jurisdiction over its dollar clearing. A firm faced with a choice between a European fine it might contest over several years and exclusion from the dollar system tomorrow is not really facing a choice at all. That is the gap I want to draw the Minister's attention to, because I think it is an oversight rather than a deliberate choice, and it can be fixed at Committee Stage with a short amendment. Consider how this will operate. An employer is required to display a policy setting out how tips are shared. Suppose that policy allocates sixty per cent of electronic tips to the kitchen, thirty per cent to the floor and ten per cent to management. A worker who thinks that is unfair has no remedy, because the employer has complied: it has a policy, it has displayed it, and it is distributing in accordance with it. The right to redress bites only if the distribution departs from the policy. So an employer who writes a policy that retains a substantial share for the house, or that allocates on a basis that disadvantages part-time or agency staff, is entirely within the law, and the workers have nothing to bring to the Commission. I do not think that is what was intended. The Bill is built on the principle that tips belong to the workers, and if that principle means anything, then the terms on which they are divided must themselves be subject to some standard of fairness and some route of challenge. My suggested amendment would provide that the policy must be fair and reasonable having regard to the contribution of the various categories of staff, that it must be arrived at following consultation with the workers concerned, and that a dispute about the policy is a matter that may be referred to the Commission in the same way as a dispute about its application.

I want to use my remaining time to make a point about that, because the tidy towns competition is often discussed as though it were a pleasant civic ornament, and it is considerably more than that. In practice, the committees that enter this competition are doing work that would otherwise fall to the local authority or would not be done at all. They are maintaining planting schemes, running recycling initiatives, surveying biodiversity, painting derelict frontages, and in many cases they are the only functioning community organisation left in the village. When somebody needs to be brought to a hospital appointment, it is frequently one of them who does it. The competition is the scaffolding around a much broader civic infrastructure. The difficulty, and it is the reason I raise it, is that these committees are ageing. In Clonegal, as in my own village, the people doing the work are largely the same people who were doing it twenty years ago, and they are now in their seventies. When they stop, and they will stop, there is no succession. Younger people are commuting, they have childcare responsibilities, and the model of volunteering that assumes an available weekday afternoon does not fit their lives. So my question to the Minister of State is whether the Department has given any thought to supporting these committees in a way that reduces the burden rather than simply recognising the achievement. Specifically: a small grant that could fund a shared part-time coordinator across a cluster of villages, insurance cover organised centrally rather than by each committee separately, and access to local authority machinery for the heavier work. Those three things would extend the life of many committees by a decade.

I am, however, less interested in the leadership of the party opposite than in the point of substance that has been raised, and I will address it directly, because it deserves an answer rather than a joke. The shadow Minister argued that the funding formula announced yesterday will disadvantage authorities with the highest levels of deprivation. That is a serious claim and if it were true it would be a serious problem. It is not true, and I want to explain why with reference to the actual distribution rather than to assertion. The formula retains the deprivation weighting in full. What has changed is the treatment of the area cost adjustment, which reflects differences in the cost of delivering the same service in different parts of the country, principally driven by wage levels. That adjustment has not been updated in a decade and had become significantly detached from the underlying data. Updating it moves resource towards areas where costs have risen fastest, and those are not uniformly the most affluent areas; they include several coastal authorities and a number of the northern cities. If the hon. Member has an analysis showing otherwise, I would genuinely like to see it, and I will engage with it seriously and publish my officials' response. What I would ask, though, is that we conduct this argument on the basis of the published tables rather than on the basis of a briefing note. I will say one further thing. Whatever the distribution, the total quantum is what determines whether any authority can deliver its statutory duties, and I do not pretend that the settlement is generous. The pressures in adult social care and in children's services are consuming an increasing share of every authority's budget regardless of where they sit in the formula, and that is a structural problem no redistribution will solve.

That is the tradition and it is worth defending, particularly at a moment when the multilateral system is under more strain than at any point since it was constructed. I want to say something about why a country of our size should invest in it at all, because the argument is occasionally made that we are a small state, that our vote in the General Assembly counts the same as anyone else's, and that the money spent on our permanent mission and on our peacekeeping contribution might be better spent at home. I understand the argument and I reject it. Our influence in the world is not military and it will never be economic in any sense that would trouble a great power. It rests entirely on credibility, on the accumulated record of having been consistent, and on the willingness of other countries to believe that our position on a question is the position we actually hold rather than one we have been assigned. That credibility took decades to build. It is why our diplomats are asked to chair processes that matter, why we were able to play the role we did on the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, and why we secured a Security Council seat against much larger competitors. It is an asset and it can be spent, but it can also be squandered, and it is squandered by inconsistency. That brings me to the point some colleagues have raised, which is whether we apply our principles evenly. It is a fair challenge. If we invoke international law in one conflict and speak of complexity in another, then the credibility I have described begins to erode, and the countries watching us are perfectly capable of noticing. I would rather we were consistent and occasionally uncomfortable.

So the riders know they are untouchable, and they perform accordingly. Our Bill addressed this at the point of supply and possession rather than at the point of pursuit: registration of these vehicles at sale, an offence of possession in a public place without insurance and protective equipment, and clear powers of seizure and disposal without the current requirement to establish the identity of the rider. We heard about what happened to families over generations, and we heard it in the words of people who lived it, which is not the same as reading it in a report. My critique is this. Having heard all of that, and having received ninety-four calls to action, this House has developed a habit of responding to each anniversary with a debate in which we quote the commission back to each other. The quoting is sincere. I do not question anybody's sincerity. But sincerity is not implementation, and the tracking that independent organizations have done shows that the number of calls fully implemented remains a small fraction of the total, years after we committed to all of them without qualification. I want to be specific rather than general, because generality is part of the problem. Call to action nineteen asks for the annual publication of health outcome data comparing Indigenous and non-Indigenous populations, with measurable goals to close the gaps. That is not expensive. It requires no negotiation with any province about jurisdiction over anything. It requires a department to compile numbers it largely already holds and publish them on a schedule. It has not been done consistently. Call to action fifty-three, on the national council for reconciliation, took eight years to reach legislation. Meanwhile the water advisories that were to be lifted by a stated date were not lifted by that date, and the residential school records that survivors have sought remain contested in litigation that this government has continued to fund. So when I hear a minister say that reconciliation is a journey and not a destination, I understand the sentiment and I distrust the usage, because a journey with no arrival date and no odometer is indistinguishable from standing still. Publish the tracker. Fund the records. Lift the advisories.
